title: Double your productivity: eliminate low-velocity time instead of chasing 1% daily gains
summary: Jason Cohen debunks the "1% better per day = 37x" idea and shows why a one-time 2-3x productivity gain is still achievable. Using an average-speed puzzle, he argues low-velocity activity (email, idle meetings, calendar management) drags down your average, so the lever is eliminating it, measured with a tool like RescueTime, not working harder.

principles.text: Compounding 1% daily improvement in productivity is unrealistic; other factors overwhelm the simplistic math.
principles.quote: Things rarely compound like that, even at slow rates. Or at least, there are other factors that overwhelm that simplistic idea.

principles.text: Low-velocity periods wash away high-velocity gains, so your average is dominated by your slow time.
principles.quote: It's amazing how periods of low velocity wash away gains of high velocity.

principles.text: You can't make up for lost time with bursts of speed; when half your day is slow, the other half can't compensate.
principles.quote: When half your day moves at 30 mph, it's impossible to make up the time during the other half.

principles.text: The biggest productivity lever is eliminating low-velocity work (useless email, idle meetings, calendar management), not speeding up what you already do well.
principles.quote: Once you realize that the low-velocity stuff is responsible for most of the drag on your productivity, you realize that the thing to do is eliminate the low-velocity stuff.

principles.text: Measure where your time actually goes with a tool like RescueTime; seeing the numbers makes correction easy.
principles.quote: Once you see the numbers it's easy to correct.

principles.text: Roughly doubling productivity is achievable without longer hours or more stress: stop averaging down, and make sure your big-rock tasks are the right ones.
principles.quote: The best part is, none of this means working late or working harder. Just stop averaging down!
